title: Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and Dispersion

toc.title: 12.1 Reflection at curved mirrors: mirror formula and magnification
12.2 Refraction at plane surfaces, critical angle and TIR; refraction through a prism
12.3 Lenses: lens formula, lens maker's formula, power and combinations

html:
Ray optics is the chapter of straight lines: rays, normals, angles and images. The Waves and Optics area carries 8 of the 50 Physics questions (official MEC weightage), and we estimate about 3 of them come from this chapter.

Almost every question is one of five calculations — a mirror or lens position, an apparent depth, a critical angle, a prism deviation, or the power of a combination — and almost every lost mark comes from a sign.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • The Cartesian sign convention, once: distances from the pole or optical centre, positive along the incident light. Concave mirror f<0, convex mirror f>0; convex lens f>0, concave lens f<0; a real object has u<0.
  • Mirror: \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}, m = -\frac{v}{u}, R = 2f.
  • Lens: \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}, m = \frac{v}{u}.
  • Refraction: \mu = c/v, \mu_1\sin i = \mu_2\sin r; apparent depth = real depth /\mu; \sin C = 1/\mu; TIR needs dense \to rare and i > C.
  • Prism: A = r_1 + r_2, \delta = i_1 + i_2 - A, \mu = \frac{\sin((A+\delta_m)/2)}{\sin(A/2)}, thin prism \delta = (\mu-1)A.
  • Lens maker: \frac{1}{f} = (\mu-1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right); power P = 1/f in dioptre.
  • Combinations: P = P_1 + P_2 in contact only; separated by d, P = P_1 + P_2 - dP_1P_2.
  • Dispersion: \mu falls as \lambda rises, so violet deviates most; \omega = \frac{\mu_v - \mu_r}{\mu_y - 1}; achromatism needs \frac{\omega_1}{f_1} + \frac{\omega_2}{f_2} = 0.

12.1 Reflection at curved mirrors: mirror formula and magnification

The laws of reflection

  1. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection: i = r.
  2. The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane.

Both angles are measured from the normal, not from the surface.

A spherical mirror is part of a hollow sphere.

Its pole P is the centre of its surface, its centre of curvature C the centre of that sphere, and its principal focus F the point where rays parallel to the principal axis converge (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex) after reflection.

The radius of curvature is R = 2f, and the focal length is half the radius — a fact worth memorising on its own.

Concave mirror Convex mirror
Reflecting surface inner (hollow) side outer (bulging) side
Effect on parallel rays converges them to F diverges them, as if from F behind
Focal length real focus, in front virtual focus, behind
Images real or virtual, depending on the object distance always virtual, erect, diminished
Uses shaving mirror, headlight reflector, dentist's mirror, solar cooker rear-view mirror, security mirror, blind corners
The Cartesian sign convention — stated once, used throughout

Take the pole (mirror) or optical centre (lens) as the origin, and the principal axis as the x-axis. Measure every distance from the origin, and take the direction of the incident light as positive.

For a mirror the light travels towards the mirror, so the object side is negative: u<0 for a real object, and a real image in front of the mirror also has v<0. A concave mirror has its focus in front, so f<0; a convex mirror has its focus behind, so f>0.

Heights are positive above the axis. A positive magnification means an erect image; a negative magnification means an inverted one.

The mirror formula

\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}, \qquad m = \frac{h'}{h} = -\frac{v}{u}

u is the object distance, v the image distance, f the focal length, h the object height and h' the image height.

The formula holds for concave and convex mirrors alike, for real and virtual objects and images, provided the signs are put in correctly. It is accurate only for paraxial rays (a small aperture).

The mirror formula

Setting up. An object BQ stands on the axis, its foot B at distance u from the pole and its tip Q at height h.

A ray from Q parallel to the axis hits the mirror at M and reflects through F; a second ray from Q through F reflects parallel to the axis.

They meet at Q', the image tip, at distance v from the pole with height h' above the image foot B'. Take all lengths as magnitudes for now.

Step 1 — the ray through the focus. The triangles Q'B'F and MPF are similar (MP is the mirror height where the parallel ray strikes). The parallel ray keeps its height, so MP = h, and

\frac{h'}{h} = \frac{v - f}{f}

Step 2 — the ray through the pole. The triangles Q'B'P and QBP are similar, because the ray through the pole is undeviated and the two verticals are parallel:

\frac{h'}{h} = \frac{v}{u}

Step 3 — equate the two expressions.

\frac{v}{u} = \frac{v-f}{f} \;\Rightarrow\; vf = uv - uf

Step 4 — divide every term by uvf.

\frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{v} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}

Result. \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}.

What it means. The magnitudes above were used only for a real image of a concave mirror.

Because every distance is measured from the pole with a sign, the same equation covers virtual images, convex mirrors and virtual objects without change — provided the signs go in.

Conditions: paraxial rays only (small aperture), and a thin mirror.

The examiner is looking for

The sign convention written down before substitution, the formula, the substitution with signs, and the statement "real, inverted, magnified" — not just a number.

A bare answer of "30 cm" earns half the marks; "30 cm in front of the mirror, real and inverted" earns all of them.

Where the image forms

For a concave mirror:

Object position Image position Nature
at infinity at F real, inverted, highly diminished (a point)
beyond C between F and C real, inverted, diminished
at C at C real, inverted, same size (m = -1)
between C and F beyond C real, inverted, magnified
at F at infinity real, inverted, infinitely magnified
between F and P behind the mirror virtual, erect, magnified

A convex mirror gives a virtual, erect, diminished image between P and F for every real object, which is exactly why it is used as a rear-view mirror: a wide field of view in a small, upright image.

Worked example 12.1 — a concave mirror

Problem. An object is 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the position, nature and magnification of the image.

Solution. Convention: u = -15 cm, f = -10 cm. \dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{15} = \dfrac{-3+2}{30} = -\dfrac{1}{30}, so v = -30 cm.

The image is 30 cm in front of the mirror — real (negative v), and m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{-30}{-15} = -2: inverted and twice the size.

Four sign traps in mirrors
  1. Concave f is negative in this convention. Using f = +10 with u = -15 gives v = +6 — a virtual image where a real one belongs.
  2. A positive v means behind the mirror: the image is virtual and cannot be caught on a screen.
  3. m = -v/u, not v/u. The minus sign is what tells you the image is inverted.
  4. R = 2f, so a mirror of radius 40 cm has f = 20 cm, not 40.

12.2 Refraction at plane surfaces, critical angle and TIR; refraction through a prism

Refraction and Snell's law

Refraction is the change in direction of light when it crosses a boundary between two transparent media, caused by a change in its speed. The frequency does not change; the wavelength does.

\mu = \frac{c}{v}, \qquad \mu_1\sin i = \mu_2\sin r

\mu is the absolute refractive index of a medium (relative to vacuum), c the speed of light in vacuum and v the speed in that medium.

For two media, \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{\mu_2}{\mu_1} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2}: light bends towards the normal on entering a denser medium and away from it on leaving.

Medium \mu Speed of light (m s⁻¹)
vacuum / air 1 (1.0003) 3.0\times10^8
water 1.33 2.25\times10^8
crown glass 1.52 1.97\times10^8
diamond 2.42 1.24\times10^8

Real and apparent depth

A pool looks shallower than it is, and a coin at the bottom of a glass of water looks raised. The rule is simple:

\text{apparent depth} = \frac{\text{real depth}}{\mu}

so the shift is t\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\mu}\right) for a layer of thickness t.

Apparent depth

Setting up. An object O lies a real depth d below a plane surface; the observer is in air above. Take a ray from O that reaches the surface at a small angle of incidence i (measured in the liquid) and leaves at angle r in air.

Step 1 — Snell's law. \mu\sin i = 1\cdot\sin r.

Step 2 — small angles. For a ray close to the normal, \sin i \approx \tan i and \sin r \approx \tan r, so \mu\tan i = \tan r.

Step 3 — geometry. If the ray leaves the surface a horizontal distance x from the point above the object, then \tan i = x/d and \tan r = x/d', where d' is where the backward extension of the emergent ray meets the vertical.

Step 4 — substitute. \mu\dfrac{x}{d} = \dfrac{x}{d'}, so d' = d/\mu.

Result. The object appears at the apparent depth d/\mu, i.e. raised.

Conditions. Near-normal viewing, observer in the rarer medium, flat surface. Viewing at a steep angle makes the bottom look curved and the simple rule fails.

Worked example 12.2 — how deep is the tank?

Problem. A water tank is 4.0 m deep (\mu = 4/3). How deep does it look from directly above? How much does the bottom appear to be raised?

Solution. d' = d/\mu = 4.0/(4/3) = 3.0 m. Shift = 4.0 - 3.0 = 1.0 m, which also follows from t(1 - 1/\mu) = 4(1 - 3/4) = 1 m.

Through a slab. A ray crossing a parallel-sided glass slab emerges parallel to its original direction but displaced sideways by

\text{lateral shift} = \frac{t\,\sin(i-r)}{\cos r}

The slab changes the path but not the direction — that is why a window pane does not distort what you see through it.

Critical angle and total internal reflection

When light travels from a denser to a rarer medium it bends away from the normal, so the angle of refraction is larger than the angle of incidence.

At a particular angle of incidence the refracted ray grazes the surface (r = 90^{\circ}); beyond it there is no refracted ray at all and the light is totally internally reflected.

\sin C = \frac{1}{\mu} \qquad (\text{denser} \to \text{air})

Medium \mu Critical angle
water 1.33 48.6°
crown glass 1.52 41.1°
flint glass 1.62 38.1°
diamond 2.42 24.4°

Two conditions for TIR, and both are needed:

  1. light must be travelling from a denser to a rarer medium;
  2. the angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle.

A larger \mu means a smaller critical angle, which is why diamond sparkles: its critical angle is only 24.4°, so most light entering it is totally reflected several times before escaping.

Where TIR is used

  • Optical fibres. A core of high \mu is surrounded by a cladding of slightly lower \mu; light entering at a small angle strikes the core–cladding boundary at an angle far above the critical angle and is totally reflected again and again, following the fibre around bends with almost no loss. This carries telephone, internet and TV signals, and lets an endoscope look inside the body.
  • Mirage. On a hot road the air near the ground is hotter and less dense, so its \mu is slightly lower than the cooler air above. Rays from the sky bend gradually and are totally reflected near the ground, so the road appears to be covered with water.
  • Prism periscope and binoculars. A right-angled isosceles prism reflects light through 90° (or 180°) by TIR at its hypotenuse, where i = 45^{\circ} exceeds the critical angle of glass. Prisms are used instead of mirrors because there is no silvering to tarnish and no double image from a front and a back surface.
  • Diamond sparkle, and the light pipe used to carry light into a room.

Refraction through a prism

A prism is a transparent body with two plane refracting faces meeting at the refracting angle A (the angle of the prism). A ray entering one face and leaving the other is bent twice, both times towards the base, through a total angle of deviation \delta.

A = r_1 + r_2, \qquad \delta = i_1 + i_2 - A

where i_1 is the angle of incidence at the first face, r_1 the angle of refraction there, r_2 the angle of incidence at the second face and i_2 the angle of emergence.

The prism relations

Setting up. The ray meets the first face at Q and leaves the second face at R. The normals at Q and R meet at N, and A is the apex.

Step 1 — the quadrilateral. In quadrilateral AQNR the angles at Q and R are 90^{\circ} each, so \angle QNR = 180^{\circ} - A.

Step 2 — the triangle QNR. Its angles are r_1, r_2 and 180^{\circ} - A, and they add to 180^{\circ}:

r_1 + r_2 = A

Step 3 — deviation at each face. At the first face the ray is turned by i_1 - r_1; at the second by i_2 - r_2. The two turns are in the same sense, so

\delta = (i_1 - r_1) + (i_2 - r_2) = i_1 + i_2 - (r_1 + r_2) = i_1 + i_2 - A

Result. A = r_1 + r_2 and \delta = i_1 + i_2 - A.

Conditions. A triangular prism in air, with the ray crossing both faces (not totally reflected at the second).

Minimum deviation

As the angle of incidence is increased from zero, \delta first falls, reaches a minimum \delta_m, then rises again. At the minimum the path is symmetrical: the ray passes through the prism parallel to the base, and

i_1 = i_2 = i, \qquad r_1 = r_2 = \frac{A}{2}, \qquad \delta_m = 2i - A

so i = \dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2}, and Snell's law at either face gives the prism formula

\mu = \frac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A+\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}

For a thin prism (A a few degrees) the sines can be replaced by their angles, and the result collapses to

\delta = (\mu - 1)A

which is the form used for small-angle prisms in spectacles and rangefinders.

Worked example 12.3 — refractive index from a prism

Problem. A prism of angle 60° gives a minimum deviation of 30°. Find \mu.

Solution. i = \dfrac{A+\delta_m}{2} = \dfrac{60+30}{2} = 45^{\circ} and r = A/2 = 30^{\circ}, so \mu = \dfrac{\sin 45^{\circ}}{\sin 30^{\circ}} = \dfrac{0.707}{0.500} = 1.41.

Prism traps
  1. \delta = i_1 + i_2 - A is not \delta_m; it is the deviation for that particular ray. Only at minimum deviation is i_1 = i_2.
  2. At minimum deviation r = A/2, not A. Using r = 60^{\circ} in the formula gives nonsense.
  3. The thin-prism result \delta = (\mu-1)A is a small-angle approximation. It is good to about 1 % for A below 10°, and \delta comes out in whatever unit A is given in — degrees with degrees, radians with radians.

12.3 Lenses: lens formula, lens maker's formula, power and combinations

A lens is a transparent medium bounded by two refracting surfaces. A convex (biconvex) lens is thicker at the middle and converges parallel rays to a real focus; a concave (biconcave) lens is thinner at the middle and diverges them, so its focus is virtual.

Convex (converging) Concave (diverging)
Shape thicker at the centre thinner at the centre
Effect on parallel rays converges to a real focus diverges, as if from a virtual focus
Focal length (convention) positive negative
Power positive negative
Images of a real object real or virtual, depending on distance always virtual, erect, diminished

The lens formula

With the same Cartesian convention as §12.1 (distances from the optical centre, positive along the incident light, real object u<0):

\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}, \qquad m = \frac{h'}{h} = \frac{v}{u}

Note the difference from the mirror: a minus before 1/u, and no minus in m.

For a convex lens with u = -30 cm and f = 20 cm, \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{20} - \frac{1}{30} = \frac{1}{60}, so v = +60 cm — a real image 60 cm beyond the lens, with m = 60/(-30) = -2: inverted and twice as large.

Object position (convex lens) Image position Nature
at infinity at F real, inverted, a point
beyond 2F between F and 2F real, inverted, diminished
at 2F at 2F real, inverted, same size (m = -1)
between F and 2F beyond 2F real, inverted, magnified
at F at infinity real, inverted, infinitely magnified
between F and the lens same side virtual, erect, magnified

A concave lens gives a virtual, erect, diminished image between the lens and F for every real object.

The lens maker's formula

The focal length of a thin lens is fixed by its material and its two surfaces:

\frac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)

R_1 is the radius of the first surface (the one the light meets first) and R_2 the second, each positive if that surface bulges towards the incident light.

For a biconvex lens R_1 > 0 and R_2 < 0, so both terms add; for a biconcave lens R_1 < 0 and R_2 > 0, so f comes out negative.

Power

The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length in metres:

P = \frac{1}{f\ (\text{in metres})}, \qquad \text{unit: dioptre (D)} = \text{m}^{-1}

A converging lens has positive power, a diverging lens negative. f = +25 cm gives P = +4 D; f = -50 cm gives P = -2 D. Opticians write a prescription in dioptres because powers, unlike focal lengths, simply add.

Combinations of lenses

In contact. For thin lenses touching each other, the powers add:

P = P_1 + P_2 + P_3 + \cdots, \qquad \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2}

so a +5 D and a -2 D lens in contact behave as a single +3 D lens of focal length 100/3 = 33.3 cm.

Separated by a distance d. The formula changes:

P = P_1 + P_2 - dP_1P_2, \qquad \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2} - \frac{d}{f_1f_2}

with d in metres. The extra term appears because the second lens receives the image of the first as its object, and the two lens equations combine to give -\dfrac{d}{f_1f_2}.

A +5 D and a -5 D lens in contact give P = 0 (no net power), but separated by 20 cm they give P = 0 - (0.2)(5)(-5) = +5 D — a converging combination. The separation term is not a detail; it is the whole answer.

Magnification of a combination is the product: m = m_1\times m_2.

Worked example 12.4 — two lenses in contact

Problem. A convex lens of power +5 D and a concave lens of power −2 D are placed in contact. Find the power and focal length of the combination, and its nature.

Solution. P = P_1 + P_2 = 5 + (-2) = +3 D. f = 1/P = 1/3\ \text{m} = 33.3 cm, positive, so the combination is converging. The two lenses share the same axis and the same image position; only the powers add.

Worked example 12.5 — the same lenses, 20 cm apart

Problem. A convex lens of power +5 D and a concave lens of power -5 D are mounted on one axis, 20 cm apart. Find the equivalent power and focal length, and compare with the result when they touch.

Solution. In contact, P = 5 + (-5) = 0 and f = \infty: the pair behaves like a plain glass plate. Separated by d = 0.20 m, P = P_1 + P_2 - dP_1P_2 = 0 - (0.20)(5)(-5) = +5 D, so f = 1/5 = 0.20 m = 20 cm, converging.

Moving the lenses apart has turned a powerless pair into a +5 D combination — the separation term is as large as either power.

The three lens traps
  1. P = P_1 + P_2 holds only in contact. Separated by d, the power is P_1 + P_2 - dP_1P_2. Two lenses of +5 D and -5 D are powerless in contact but +5 D when 20 cm apart.
  2. A converging lens in water is weaker. The lens maker's formula uses \mu_{\text{lens}}/\mu_{\text{medium}} - 1, not \mu - 1. Glass (\mu = 1.5) in water (\mu = 4/3) has 1/f smaller by a factor \dfrac{1.5/1.333 - 1}{1.5 - 1} = \dfrac{0.125}{0.5} = \frac{1}{4}, so the focal length becomes four times longer. A lens of \mu less than the liquid's would even change from converging to diverging.
  3. m = v/u, not -v/u, for a lens. The mirror formula has the minus; the lens formula does not.

12.4 Dispersion, chromatic aberration and achromatism

Dispersion

Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its component colours by refraction. It happens because the refractive index of a material is not the same for all wavelengths: it is largest for violet and smallest for red.

\mu_{\text{violet}} > \mu_{\text{yellow}} > \mu_{\text{red}}

Since \delta = (\mu-1)A for a thin prism, violet is deviated most and red least, so a prism spreads white light into a band — the spectrum, in the order VIBGYOR (violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red) from the most deviated end.

The physical reason is speed: in glass, violet travels more slowly than red, so it bends more. In vacuum all colours travel at the same speed and there is no dispersion.

Two numbers describe the spreading:

Quantity Formula Meaning
Angular dispersion \delta_v - \delta_r = (\mu_v - \mu_r)A the angle between the violet and red rays after a thin prism
Dispersive power \omega = \dfrac{\mu_v - \mu_r}{\mu_y - 1} how strongly the material spreads colours, independent of A

\omega is a property of the material alone — about 0.017 for crown glass and 0.030 for flint glass. That is why flint glass is used for the dispersing prism of a spectrometer and crown glass for the lenses.

Chromatic aberration

A lens behaves like a stack of prisms, so it too disperses. Rays of different colours come to focus at different points: violet focuses nearest the lens (it is bent most) and red farthest. This defect is chromatic aberration.

  • Longitudinal (axial) aberration: the images lie along the axis at different distances, so a white object has a coloured blur.
  • Lateral (transverse) aberration: the images have different sizes, so the edges of a white object are fringed with colour even when the centre is sharp.

A mirror does not suffer from chromatic aberration: reflection does not depend on wavelength. That is why large astronomical telescopes are reflectors.

Achromatism

A combination of two lenses can cancel the dispersion while keeping some net power. For two thin lenses in contact, the condition for an achromatic doublet is

\frac{\omega_1}{f_1} + \frac{\omega_2}{f_2} = 0 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \frac{f_1}{f_2} = -\frac{\omega_1}{\omega_2}

The powers must have opposite signs — one converging, one diverging — and the ratio of focal lengths must equal the inverse ratio of dispersive powers.

Since flint glass has about twice the dispersive power of crown glass, the flint element must have about twice the focal length of the crown element, and therefore half its power.

The combination is achromatic but not free of spherical aberration, and its net power is only about half that of the converging element alone.

Worked example 12.6 — dispersive power

Problem. A glass has \mu_v = 1.53, \mu_r = 1.51 and \mu_y = 1.52. Find its dispersive power and the angular dispersion of a 10° prism of this glass.

Solution. \omega = \dfrac{1.53-1.51}{1.52-1} = \dfrac{0.02}{0.52} = 0.038. Angular dispersion = (\mu_v - \mu_r)A = 0.02\times10^{\circ} = 0.2^{\circ}.

Reading an optics question

Write the convention first, then list the three knowns with signs, then choose the formula. In a combination question ask at once: in contact or separated? In a "which defect" question ask: lens or mirror? These two questions settle most of the chapter.

Formula and fact sheet

Topic Formula or fact

Mirror formula \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}; m = -\frac{v}{u}
Sign convention origin at pole/optical centre; + along the incident light; real object u<0; concave mirror f<0; convex mirror f>0

Convex mirror always virtual, erect, diminished, between P and F

Critical angle \sin C = 1/\mu; water 48.6°, crown glass 41.1°, diamond 24.4°
TIR denser \to rarer and i > C
Prism A = r_1 + r_2; \delta = i_1 + i_2 - A

Lens formula \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}; m = \frac{v}{u}

Lenses in contact P = P_1 + P_2; \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2}; m = m_1m_2
Lenses separated P = P_1 + P_2 - dP_1P_2
Lens in water \frac{1}{f} = \left(\frac{\mu_l}{\mu_m}-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R_1}-\frac{1}{R_2}\right); glass in water: f becomes 4 times
Dispersion \mu falls as \lambda rises; violet deviates most; VIBGYOR
Dispersive power \omega = \frac{\mu_v-\mu_r}{\mu_y-1}; angular dispersion = (\mu_v-\mu_r)A
Achromatism \frac{\omega_1}{f_1} + \frac{\omega_2}{f_2} = 0; crown + flint, opposite signs
Chromatic aberration violet focus nearest the lens; mirrors are free of it

Chapter summary

  • The Cartesian convention fixes everything: origin at the pole or optical centre, positive along the incident light; a real object has u<0, a concave mirror f<0, a convex lens f>0.
  • Mirror: \frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f} and m=-\frac{v}{u}; R = 2f; a convex mirror is always virtual, erect and diminished.
  • Refraction: \mu = c/v and \mu_1\sin i = \mu_2\sin r; frequency is unchanged at a boundary, wavelength and speed are not.
  • Apparent depth = d/\mu; a slab shifts the ray sideways without changing its direction; \sin C = 1/\mu, and TIR needs dense-to-rare plus i>C.
  • Prism: A = r_1+r_2 and \delta = i_1+i_2-A; at minimum deviation the ray is symmetrical and \mu = \sin((A+\delta_m)/2)/\sin(A/2); a thin prism gives \delta = (\mu-1)A.
  • Lens: \frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f}, m=\frac{v}{u}, \frac{1}{f}=(\mu-1)(1/R_1-1/R_2), P = 1/f in dioptres.
  • In contact P = P_1+P_2; separated by d, P = P_1+P_2-dP_1P_2. A converging lens in water has a longer focal length — about four times longer for glass.
  • Dispersion: \mu falls as \lambda rises, so violet bends most; \omega measures the spread; a crown–flint doublet with \omega_1/f_1+\omega_2/f_2=0 is achromatic, and mirrors never show chromatic aberration.

Practice questions

Answers and explanations — Set A

1.(a) — \frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f} for every spherical mirror. Option(b) is the lens formula, where the sign before 1/u differs.

2. (c) — m = h'/h = -v/u. The minus sign is what marks an inverted image; dropping it is the commonest error in the chapter.

3. (b) — a concave mirror has its focus in front of it, on the side from which the light comes, which is the negative direction in the convention.

4. (d) — the reflected rays always diverge, so the image is virtual, erect and smaller than the object, lying between the pole and the focus.

5. (a) — u = -2f gives v = -2f: the image is at C, real, inverted and the same size.

6. (c) — u = -f gives 1/v = 0, so v = \infty: the reflected rays are parallel.

7. (b) — \mu = c/v, the ratio of the speed in vacuum to the speed in the medium. It is always at least 1.

8. (d) — at the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the surface, so r = 90^{\circ} and \mu\sin C = 1\cdot\sin 90^{\circ} = 1.

9. (a) — both conditions are needed: denser to rarer, and beyond C. At exactly C the ray grazes the surface rather than being reflected.

10. (c) — the object appears raised to d/\mu. Option (a) would make the tank look deeper, which never happens.

11. (b) — the ray is turned by (i_1-r_1) and again by (i_2-r_2), and r_1+r_2 = A, giving \delta = i_1+i_2-A.

12. (d) — the symmetrical path at minimum deviation passes parallel to the base of the prism.

13. (a) — in the quadrilateral formed by the two normals and the two faces, \angle QNR = 180^{\circ}-A, and the triangle QNR gives r_1+r_2 = A.

14. (c) — for small angles \delta = (\mu-1)A; the deviation grows with \mu and with the prism angle.

15. (b) — power is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres, P = 1/f.

16. (d) — one dioptre is one reciprocal metre, \text{D} = \text{m}^{-1}.

17. (a) — \frac{1}{f} = (\mu-1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1}-\frac{1}{R_2}\right), with R_2 negative for a biconvex lens so that the two terms add.

18. (c) — powers add for thin lenses in contact. They do not multiply and they do not subtract.

19. (b) — \mu varies with \lambda, so each colour leaves the prism at a slightly different angle. In vacuum all colours travel at the same speed.

20. (d) — violet has the shortest wavelength and the largest refractive index, so it is deviated most.

21. (a) — refraction depends on wavelength, so lenses disperse; mirrors reflect all wavelengths equally.

22. (c) — an achromatic doublet brings two colours to the same focus, removing chromatic aberration.

23. (b) — \omega = (\mu_v-\mu_r)/(\mu_y-1), a pure number characteristic of the material.

24. (d) — a plane mirror gives a virtual, erect image of the same size, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

25. (c) — v = c/\mu = 3.0\times10^8/(4/3) = 2.25\times10^8 m s⁻¹.

26. (a) — light strikes the hypotenuse at 45°, which exceeds the critical angle of glass (about 42°), so it is totally reflected through 90°.

27. (b) — a plane mirror has infinite radius, so f = R/2 is infinite: parallel rays come back parallel.

28. (d) — a convex lens converges light to a real focus on the far side, the positive direction.

1. (c) — inside the focus a concave mirror gives a virtual, erect, magnified image, so the face looks larger and the right way up.

2. (a) — a convex mirror always gives an erect, diminished image between P and F, and its wide field of view shows more traffic.

9. (a) — a doublet made of two glasses of different dispersive power brings two colours to a common focus.

10. (c) — smaller speed means larger refractive index, and a larger \mu means a larger deviation.

11. (d) — inside the focus the reflected rays diverge; traced backwards they give a virtual, erect, magnified image behind the mirror.

14. (c) — f = 1/P = 1/(-2.5) = -0.40 m = -40 cm: a diverging lens.

16. (d) — the apparent thickness is t/\mu, so the object appears raised by t - t/\mu = t(1-1/\mu).

17. (a) — dispersion is the splitting by wavelength; deviation is the bending of the whole beam, and diffraction is the spreading by an obstacle.

Group D — Model answers for long questions (10 marks each, for deeper revision)

  1. Explain refraction, total internal reflection and the optical fibre. Derive the prism formula and solve a numerical. [10]
  2. Derive the lens formula and lens maker's formula, and explain dispersion with a numerical. [10]

Model answer D1: refraction, total internal reflection and the prism (10 marks)

Introduction. Refraction is the bending of light at the boundary of two media because its speed changes. Snell's law: \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = {}_1n_2 = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2}, where n = c/v is the refractive index.

Total internal reflection (TIR). When light goes from a denser to a rarer medium, the angle of refraction exceeds the angle of incidence.

At the critical angle C the refracted ray grazes the surface, with \sin C = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac1n (rarer medium air). For i > C all the light is reflected.

Conditions: (1) the light goes from a denser to a rarer medium; (2) the angle of incidence is greater than C.

Applications of TIR. Optical fibre (core n_1 greater than cladding n_2), endoscope, diamond sparkle, mirage, totally reflecting prisms in binoculars and periscopes, and the shine of an air bubble in water.

Prism. For a prism of angle A, the angle of deviation is \delta = i + e - A. The deviation is minimum when the ray passes symmetrically (i = e, r_1 = r_2 = A/2) and

n = \frac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac A2\right)}

For a thin prism (A small), \delta = (n - 1)A. The i-\delta graph is a U-shaped curve with a minimum at \delta_m.

Medium n Critical angle (to air)
Water 1.33 48.8^{\circ}
Crown glass 1.5 41.8^{\circ}
Diamond 2.42 24.4^{\circ}

Numerical. For glass with n = 1.5: \sin C = 1/1.5 gives C = 41.8^{\circ}. For a 60^{\circ} prism of the same glass, \sin\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2} = 1.5\sin30^{\circ} = 0.75, so \dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2} = 48.6^{\circ} and \delta_m = 37.2^{\circ}.

Conclusion. TIR needs a denser-to-rarer path with i > C, and a prism gives its minimum deviation when the ray passes symmetrically.

Model answer D2: lens formula, lens maker's formula and dispersion (10 marks)

Introduction. A lens refracts light at two spherical surfaces. For a thin lens we use the Cartesian sign convention, with distances measured from the optical centre and positive in the direction of the incident light.

Lens formula. \dfrac1v - \dfrac1u = \dfrac1f. The linear magnification is m = \dfrac vu. For a real image m < 0 (inverted).

Lens maker's formula. \dfrac1f = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac1{R_1} - \dfrac1{R_2}\right), where n is the refractive index of the lens relative to the medium.

Immersing a glass lens in a liquid of higher index makes a convex lens behave as a concave one. The power is P = 1/f in dioptre (f in metres). For lenses in contact P = P_1 + P_2.

Dispersion. White light splits into seven colours because n depends on wavelength (violet bends most, red least). The dispersive power is \omega = \dfrac{n_v - n_r}{n_y - 1}.

A combination of two prisms of different glass can give dispersion without deviation (achromatic) or deviation without dispersion.

A single lens has chromatic aberration (colour fringes), corrected by an achromatic doublet, with \dfrac{\omega_1}{f_1} + \dfrac{\omega_2}{f_2} = 0.

Defect Cause Cure
Spherical aberration marginal rays focus nearer stop, parabolic mirror
Chromatic aberration n varies with colour achromatic doublet
Myopia image in front of retina concave lens
Hypermetropia image behind retina convex lens

Numerical. A convex lens has f = 20\ \text{cm} and an object is placed 30\ \text{cm} away: \dfrac1v = \dfrac1{20} - \dfrac1{30} = \dfrac1{60}, so v = 60\ \text{cm} and m = 60/(-30) = -2: real, inverted, twice as large.

For a double-convex lens of glass n = 1.5 and R_1 = 20\ \text{cm}, R_2 = -20\ \text{cm}, \dfrac1f = 0.5\times\dfrac2{20}, so f = 20\ \text{cm} and P = +5\ \text{D}.

Conclusion. The lens formula and lens maker's formula together link the image position to the shape and material of the lens, and dispersion arises because n varies with colour.
